aliases: Hong Kong milk tea with condensed milk
processing: Hong Kong-style milk tea, a strained strong black tea, made with sweetened condensed milk in place of the evaporated milk and sugar.
harvest_season: Not relevant: it is a cafe drink made to order, and no particular harvest is prized.
appearance_dry: Not sold as a dry tea; the base is the dark broken black tea usual for Hong Kong milk tea.
appearance_wet: Not applicable: the leaves stay behind in the strainer.
taste_profile: Richer, sweeter and smoother than ordinary Hong Kong milk tea, with a heavy condensed-milk creaminess over strong tea.

brewing.notes: Make strong strained black tea, then stir in condensed milk to taste. No extra sugar is needed.

vintage_note: Sold as a drink, not by year or season: you order it at a cha chaan teng. Any home version simply uses a current black tea blend.
description:
Cha jau is an order at a Hong Kong cha chaan teng: milk tea made with condensed milk. It is a variation on the city's strong strained milk tea, and it comes out noticeably thicker and sweeter.

The swap does two jobs. Condensed milk brings both the dairy and the sugar, and it blends into the drink more easily than granulated sugar, which can sit undissolved at the bottom of a cooling cup. Most versions still contain some evaporated milk.

Expect a dessert-leaning cup: creamy and sweet, with the tea holding on underneath. At home, brew the tea stronger than seems sensible, because condensed milk flattens a weak base, and add the milk gradually.

The word has spread beyond tea. Staff in Hong Kong also understand the same logic for coffee, Horlicks, Ovaltine and yuenyeung, so ask for yeung jau if you want the mixed version.
history:
The drink grew out of Hong Kong's dai pai dong and their milk tea. Early stalls mixed sugar in before serving; later cafes put sugar on the table, and the condensed-milk version made added sugar unnecessary.

The name is explained in two ways. In one, 'jau' means leaving out the sugar; in the other, it means replacing evaporated milk with condensed. The first fits the wider habit of naming what a drink goes without. The sources name no inventor or date.
